title: Master Tara Singh
hook: a schoolteacher who led the Akalis for decades

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gurdwara Act, and your line was peace won. Did you take part in something shared? Today, one of the people who led the Akalis through those years and long after. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

Some nicknames outlive the job. A coach is still Coach at the grocery store years after the last game. A nurse is still the nurse at every family dinner. In Punjab, one Sikh leader kept a classroom title long after he'd left the classroom. Not General, not President, not Sardar. Master. As in schoolmaster. He led marches, negotiated with governments and went to jail, and people kept calling him the teacher. Today: Master Tara Singh.
screen: `A NICKNAME OUTLIVES THE JOB.` → `NOT GENERAL. NOT PRESIDENT.` → `MASTER, AS IN SCHOOLMASTER.`

segments.voice: First, the choice. Tara Singh was born into a Hindu family, and as a young man he chose the Sikh path and took amrit, the Khalsa initiation. That's how his biographers tell it, and it shaped him: he came to the panth by choice, and he defended it for the rest of his life. Second, the classroom. He studied at Khalsa College in Amritsar, which we met earlier in this block, and then became a teacher and a headmaster at a Khalsa school. Teaching, for him, wasn't a stop on the way to something else. It was how he understood leading: explain, persuade, keep the students together. Third, the Akalis. When the gurdwara reform movement rose, he joined it and soon stood among its leaders. He led the Akali Dal and the SGPC for many years, through the reform campaigns and later through the hard years around the partition of Punjab. He was jailed more than once. Sikhs still argue about his politics and his decisions, and historians weigh them differently. That's a real argument, and it isn't settled here. But friends and critics alike remember the name he kept. That's today's line: the teacher-leader. Fourth, the root. The Asa di Var opens, at Ang 462 of the Guru Granth Sahib, with Guru Nanak saying he is a sacrifice to his Guru a hundred times a day, the Guru who made angels out of humans without delay. In Gurbani that gratitude belongs to the Guru. But it colors the way Sikhs speak of anyone who teaches, and it helps explain why a classroom title could become a name of respect that lasted a lifetime.
screen: `HE CHOSE THE SIKH PATH.` · `TEACHER AND HEADMASTER.` · `LEADER OF THE AKALIS.` · `A SACRIFICE TO THE GURU.` · then, large: `THE TEACHER-LEADER.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with a teacher. Sit, and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one teacher who changed something in you. It might have been a schoolteacher, a coach, a grandparent, a boss, someone at the gurdwara who showed you how to sit with the Guru Granth Sahib. Picture their face, their voice, the way they explained things. Breathe in, and remember one thing they said that stayed. Breathe out, and let a little gratitude come with it. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Master Tara Singh. A schoolteacher and headmaster who led the Akalis for decades, and was called by the teacher's title all his life. Today's word.
Your line: the teacher-leader. Today, thank a teacher: send a short message to someone who taught you, and name the one thing that stayed. Day nine hundred ninety-one.

howItsDone: Master Tara Singh is remembered among Sikhs as a leader of the Akali Dal and the SGPC through the reform years and after; his life and decisions are discussed in Sikh histories, and his name is on schools and public places in Punjab.
